passages.source_text: καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ἀκούσας γελοιάζων ἔφη Τί οὖν οἴει, Κλήμης; μὴ ὑπ’ αὐτῆς ἀνάγκης σε εἰς δούλων μοι ταγῆναι τόπον; ἐπεὶ τίς τὰς καλὰς καὶ πολλὰς σινδόνας μετὰ τῶν ἐπομένων μοι δακτυλίων καὶ ὑποδήσεων φυλάξει; τίς δὲ καὶ τὰ ἡδέα καὶ πολυτελῆ ὄψα προετοιμάσει, ἅτινα ποικίλα ὄντα πολλῶν καὶ τεχνιτῶν δεῖται μαγείρων, καὶ πάντα ἐκεῖνα ὅσα ἐκτεθηλυμμένων ἀνθρώπων ὡς θηρίῳ μεγάλῳ τῇ ἐπιθυμίᾳ ἐκ πάσης πλεονεξίας πορισθέντα ἑτοιμάζεται; πλὴν εἰ τοιαύτῃ σε προαίρεσις ὑπεισῆλθεν: ἴσως μὴ συνέντα καὶ τὸν ἐμὸν ἀγνοοῦντα βίον ὅτι ἄρτῳ μόνῳ καὶ ἐλαίαις χρῶμαι καὶ σπανίως λαχάνοις — καὶ ὅτι ἱμάτιόν μοι καὶ τριβώνιον ὑπάρχει τοῦτ’ αὐτὸ ὃ περιβέβλημαι καὶ ἑτέρου χρείαν οὐκ ἔχω οὐδὲ ἄλλων τινῶν· ἐν γὰρ τούτοις καὶ περισσεύομαι. ὁ νοῦς γάρ μου τὰ ἐκεῖ πάντα ὁρῶν αἰώνια ἀγαθὰ οὐδὲν τῶν ἐνταῦθα περιβλέπεται. πλὴν σοῦ μὲν τὴν ἀγαθὴν προαίρεσιν ἀποδέχομαι καὶ θαυμάζων ἐπαινῶ πῶς ἀνὴρ ἐκ πολυτελῶν ἐθῶν ὑπάρχων ῥᾳδίως τοῖς ἀναγκαίοις τὸν σεαυτοῦ ὑπήλλαξας βίον. ἡμεῖς γὰρ ἐκ παίδων (ἐγώ τε καὶ Ἀνδρέας ὁ σύναιμος καὶ κατὰ θεὸν ἀδελφὸς ὢν ἐμός) οὐ μόνον ἐν ὀρφανίᾳ ἀνατραφέντες, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὑπὸ πενίας καὶ κακουχίας εἰς ἐργατείαν ἐθισθέντες, εὐμαρῶς νῦν τὰς τῶν ὁδῶν φέρομεν σκύλσεις. ὅθεν εἰ ἐπείθου μοι, ἐμοὶ ἂν συγκεχωρήκεις, ἀνδρὶ ἐργάτῃ, σοὶ τὰ δούλων ἀποπληροῦν μέρη.

ἐγὼ δὲ ἀκούσας σύντρομος ἐγενόμην καὶ ἐπίδακρυς οἷον λόγον εἶπεν ἀνήρ, οὗ πάντες οἱ τῆς νῦν γενεᾶς ἄνθρωποι τῷ τῆς γνώσεως καὶ εὐσεβείας λόγῳ ἥττους τυγχάνουσιν. ὁ δὲ ἰδών με σύνδακρυν τῶν δακρύων ἐπύθετο τὴν αἰτίαν. κἀγὼ ἔφην Τί τοιοῦτον ἥμαρτον, ἵνα μοι τοιοῦτον εἴπῃς λόγον; καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ἀπεκρίνατο Εἰ μὲν κακῶς εἴρηκα τὸ δουλεῦσαί σοι, σὺ πρῶτος ἥμαρτες, τοῦτ᾿ ἐμοὶ ποιῆσαι ἀξιώσας. κἀγὼ ἔφην Οὐχ ὅμοιόν ἐστιν· ἐμοὶ μὲν γὰρ τοῦτο ποιεῖν πρέπει πάνυ, σοὶ δὲ τῷ τοῦ θεοῦ κήρυκι τὰς ἡμετέρας σώζοντι ψυχὰς χαλεπὸν τοῦτο ποιεῖν ἐμοί. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ἀπεκρίνατο Συνεθέμην ἂν σοι, ἐπεὶ ὁ κύριος ἡμῶν ὁ ἐπὶ σωτηρίᾳ παντὸς τοῦ κόσμου ἐληλυθώς, μόνος ὑπὲρ πάντας εὐγενὴς ὢν, δουλείαν ὑπέμεινεν, ἵνα ἡμᾶς πείσῃ μὴ αἰδεῖσθαι τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς ἡμῶν τὰς δούλων ποιεῖν ὑπηρεσίας, κἂν πάνυ εὐγενεῖς τυγχάνωμεν. κἀγὼ ἔφην Εἰ μὲν νομίζω σε νικῆσαι λόγῳ, ἀνόητός εἰμι· πλὴν χάριν ἔχω τῇ τοῦ θεοῦ προνοίᾳ ὅτι σὲ εἰς γονέων τόπον ἔχειν κατηξιώθην.

καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ἐπυνθάνετο Οὐδεὶς δέ σου ἀληθῶς πρὸς γένος ὑπάρχει; κἀγὼ ἀπεκρινάμην Εἰσὶν μὲν πολλοὶ καὶ μεγάλοι ἄνδρες, Καίσαρος πρὸς γένους ὄντες. ὅθεν τῷ ἐμῷ πατρὶ ὡς καὶ συντρόφῳ αὐτὸς Καῖσαρ συγγενίδα συνηρμόσατο γυναῖκα, ἀφ᾿ ἧς τρεῖς ἐγενόμεθα υἱοί, δύο μὲν πρὸ ἐμοῦ, οἳ καὶ δίδυμοι ὄντες πάνυ ὅμοιοι ἀλλήλοις ἐτύγχανον, ὡς αὐτὸς ὁ πατὴρ ἔλεγέν μοι. ἐγὼ γὰρ οὔτε αὐτοὺς. οὔτε τὴν τεκοῦσαν πάνυ ἐπίσταμαι, ἀλλ᾿ ὥσπερ δι᾿ ὀνείρων ἀμαυρὸν αὐτῶν τὸ εἶδος ἀναφέρω. ἡ μὲν οὖν μήτηρ μου Ματτιδία ἐλέγετο, ὁ δὲ πατὴρ Φαῦστος, τῶν δὲ ἀδελφῶν καὶ αὐτῶν ὁ μὲν Φαυστῖνος ἐκαλεῖτο, ὁ δὲ Φαυστινιανὸς ἐλέγετο. ἐμοῦ οὖν τρίτου ἐπιγεννηθέντος αὐτοῖς ἡ μήτηρ ὄνειρον ἑωράκει (ὥσπερ ὁ πατήρ μου ὑφηγεῖτο) ὅτι ἐὰν μὴ τοὺς διδύμους υἱοὺς αὐτῆς ἐξαυτῆς παραλαβοῦσα τὴν Ῥωμαίων πρὸς ἀποδημίαν ἐξέλθῃ πόλιν ἐπ᾿ ἔτη δέκα, πανολεθρίῳ μόρῳ ἅμα αὐτοῖς ἀποθανεῖν ἔχει.

ὁ μὲν οὖν πατὴρ φιλότεκνος ὢν σύν τε δούλοις καὶ δούλαις ἐφοδιάσας ἱκανῶς καὶ εἰς πλοῖον ἐμβαλόμενος εἰς τὰς Ἀθήνας ἅμα παιδευθησομένους ἐξέπεμψεν, ἐμὲ δὲ μόνον υἱὸν εἰς παραμυθίαν ἔσχεν μεθ᾿ ἑαυτοῦ. καὶ ἐπὶ τούτῳ εὐχαριστῶ πολλὰ ὅτι κἀμὲ ὁ ὄνειρος μὴ κεκελεύκει ἅμα τῇ μητρὶ τὴν Ῥωμαίων ἐκβῆναι πόλιν. περαιωθέντος οὖν ἐνιαυτοῦ ὁ πατὴρ ἔπεμψεν εἰς Ἀθήνας χρήματα τοῖς αὐτοῦ ἅμα τε καὶ μαθεῖν τὸ πῶς διάγουσιν. οἱ δὲ ἀπελθόντες οὐχ ὑπέστρεψαν. τρίτῳ δὲ ἐνιαυτῷ ὁ πατὴρ ἀθυμῶν ἑτέρους ἔπεμψεν ὁμοίως μετὰ ἐφοδίων, οἵτινες τετάρτῳ ἐνιαυτῷ ἦλθον ἀγγέλλοντες μήτε μου τὴν τεκοῦσαν ἢ τοὺς ἀδελφοὺς ἑωρακέναι, μήτε μὴν αὐταῖς Ἀθήναις ἐπιδεδημηκέναι μήτε ἄλλου τινὸς τῶν σὺν αὐτοῖς ἀπεληλυθότων κἂν ἴχνος εὑρηκέναι.

ὁ μὲν οὖν πατὴρ ταῦτα ἀκούσας καὶ ὑπὸ πολλῆς λύπης ἔκθαμβος γενόμενος καὶ οὐκ εἰδὼς ποῦ ὁρμήσας ἐπὶ ζήτησιν αὐτῶν γένηται, ἐμέ τε παραλαβὼν καὶ εἰς Πόρτον καταβὰς πολλῶν πυκνότερον ἐπυνθάνετο ποῦ ἕκαστος αὐτῶν εἶδεν ἢ ἤκουσεν ἀπὸ τεσσάρων ἐτῶν γενόμενον ναυφράγιον. καὶ ἄλλος ἀλλαχῇ ἔλεγεν. ὁ δὲ ἀντεπυνθάνετο εἰ ἑωράκασιν σῶμα γυναικὸς μετὰ βρεφῶν ἐκβεβρασμένον. . τῶν οὖν πολλὰ λεγόντων ἑωρακέναι πτώματα κατὰ πολλοὺς τόπους, ὁ πατὴρ ἀκούων ἐστέναξεν· πλὴν ὑπὸ σπλάγχνων θορυβούμενος ἀλόγιστα ἐπυνθάνετο, ὅτι τοσοῦτον μέγεθος θαλάττης ἐρευνᾶν ἐπειρᾶτο. πλὴν συγγνωστὸς ἦν, ὅτι τῇ πρὸς τοὺς ζητουμένους στοργῇ ἐλπίσιν ἐβουκολεῖτο κεναῖς. καὶ δὴ ποτὲ ὑπὸ φροντιστὰς ποιήσας με καὶ εἰς Ῥώμην καταλείψας δωδεκαετῆ, αὐτὸς δακρύων εἰς Πόρτον κατελθὼν καὶ εἰς πλοῖον ἐνβάς, ἀναχθεὶς ἐπὶ τὴν ζήτησιν ἐπορεύθη. καὶ ἔκτοτε εἰς τὴν σήμερον ἡμέραν οὔτε γράμματα ἐδεξάμην παρ’ αὐτοῦ οὔτε εἰ ζῇ εἴτε τέθνηκεν σαφῶς ἐπίσταμαι. μᾶλλον δὲ ὑπονοῶ ὅτι καὶ αὐτὸς τέθνηκέν που, ἢ ὑπὸ λύπης νικηθεὶς ἢ ναυφραγίῳ περιπεσών. τοῦτο δὲ δεῖγμα ὅτι ἤδη λοιπὸν ἔκτοτε εἰκοστὸν ἔτος ἐστίν, ἀφ’ ἧς οὐδεμίαν τινὰ περὶ αὐτοῦ ἀλήθειαν ἤκουσα.

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,
  Nicene Creed, Chalcedonian Definition) and replaced with a
  theological-stance section that declines specific creedal
  commitment. Translation philosophy and contested-terms table
  preserved unchanged; those are methodology, not creedal
  commitment, and the project actually runs on them. Added a
  "Translating into other languages" section stating POB's long-
  term intention to ship in every feasible major language, with
  the full revision pipeline and transparent supported-language
  disclosure. Per-verse YAML citing the old `doctrine_reference`
  values is preserved as historical record; those are not
  retroactively edited.
context.ambiguity_review_standard: Apply the supplied DOCTRINE.md ambiguity policy: a defensible contextual rendering may be used in the main text when material alternatives and the reason for the choice are preserved in notes. A unique or uncontested interpretation is not required. Distinguish (a) an unreadable or unverified source, omitted content, invented restoration, or a construction for which no defensible English can be given, from (b) ordinary lexical, attachment, or referent ambiguity faithfully preserved in English or explained with viable alternatives. The former blocks publication; the latter does not automatically block it. A note cannot excuse unsupported wording: the proposed main rendering must itself be defensible from the supplied Greek. Clearly printed gaps must remain gaps, not be filled by invention. Never change a verdict merely to achieve acceptance.
context.selected_edition_coverage_standard: Coverage is assessed against ALL SURVIVING WORDING AND PRINTED GAP MARKERS in the selected image-checked edition, not against unavailable words of a hypothetical complete original. A confirmed printed lacuna must remain an explicit gap in the English, retaining the exact number of printed dots (layout whitespace may differ), with a source-quoted note explaining that its content is unavailable and no restoration has been supplied. Such faithful representation can pass selected-edition coverage; it must never be described as recovery of the lost wording or an unbroken original. Distinguish this from missing scan pages, unverified ink, omitted surviving Greek, an unsupported English completion, or a translation that obscures the gap: those remain blocking. Neither this scope clarification nor a prior suggestion is an instruction to accept a draft; independently check every surviving clause, every gap, and every disclosure.

When Peter heard this, he said jokingly, “What then do you think, Clement? Do you suppose that by sheer necessity you are to be assigned a place among my servants? For who will look after the many fine linen garments, together with the rings and footwear that accompany me? And who will prepare the pleasant and costly foods, which, being varied, require many skilled cooks—and all those things that, procured through every kind of greed, are prepared for the desire of effeminate people as though for a huge wild beast? But if a resolve has crept into you in this way, perhaps it is because you did not understand and did not know my way of life: I subsist on bread alone and olives, and only rarely on vegetables. The garment I have—a worn cloak—is this very one I am wearing, and I have no need of another or of anything else; indeed, in these things I have more than enough. For my mind, seeing all the eternal good things there, does not look around at any of the things here.

“Nevertheless, I welcome your good resolve, and with admiration I praise how readily you, a man accustomed to luxurious habits, have changed your way of life to one of mere necessities. For from childhood we—I and Andrew, who is my brother both by blood and according to God—were not only brought up as orphans but were also accustomed by poverty and hardship to a life of labor. We therefore now bear the hardships of the roads with ease. Consequently, if you listened to me, you would permit me, a working man, to perform a servant’s duties for you.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μὴ ὑπ’ αὐτῆς ἀνάγκης σε εἰς δούλων μοι ταγῆναι τόπον;
lexical_decisions.chosen: Do you suppose that by sheer necessity you are to be assigned a place among my servants?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The μή-question is an incredulous, joking question. “Servants” follows the supplied wording policy for δοῦλος, while the underlying term can denote enslaved household members.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the many fine linen garments
lexical_decisions.rationale: σινδόνες can denote fine linen cloths or garments. The surrounding references to personal rings and footwear favor garments, though “fine linen cloths” remains possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μετὰ τῶν ἐπομένων μοι δακτυλίων καὶ ὑποδήσεων
lexical_decisions.chosen: together with the rings and footwear that accompany me
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative μοι identifies Peter as the person whom the rings and footwear accompany or with whom they are associated; it does not make them accessories belonging to the linen garments.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὅσα ἐκτεθηλυμμένων ἀνθρώπων ὡς θηρίῳ μεγάλῳ τῇ ἐπιθυμίᾳ ἐκ πάσης πλεονεξίας πορισθέντα ἑτοιμάζεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: all those things that, procured through every kind of greed, are prepared for the desire of effeminate people as though for a huge wild beast
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering retains the author’s disparaging description, the comparison of desire to a large wild beast, and the charge that these things are acquired through greed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἱμάτιόν μοι καὶ τριβώνιον ὑπάρχει τοῦτ’ αὐτὸ ὃ περιβέβλημαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: The garment I have—a worn cloak—is this very one I am wearing
lexical_decisions.rationale: τριβώνιον denotes a worn or rough cloak. The nouns are read appositionally, emphasizing that Peter possesses only the garment currently around him; alternatively, the wording could be represented more formally as “my garment and cloak are this very thing I am wearing.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: indeed, in these things I have more than enough
lexical_decisions.rationale: περισσεύομαι conveys abundance or surplus rather than mere adequacy.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ἀνδρέας ὁ σύναιμος καὶ κατὰ θεὸν ἀδελφὸς ὢν ἐμός
lexical_decisions.chosen: Andrew, who is my brother both by blood and according to God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The literal expression “according to God” is retained rather than reduced to the interpretive label “spiritual brother.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: we bear the hardships of the roads
lexical_decisions.rationale: σκύλσεις can denote vexations, harassment, or hardships. “Hardships” suits the rigors of travel without restricting the expression to one kind of difficulty.

source_issues.source_quote: πλὴν εἰ τοιαύτῃ σε προαίρεσις ὑπεισῆλθεν
source_issues.issue: The printed τοιαύτῃ is dative although προαίρεσις is nominative. The main translation provisionally understands τοιαύτῃ adverbially, “in this way.” A conjectural nominative τοιαύτη would instead give the more regular construction “if such a resolve has crept into you.” The image-checked printed reading has not been altered.
source_issues.proposed_reading: πλὴν εἰ τοιαύτη σε προαίρεσις ὑπεισῆλθεν

passages.text:
When I heard this, I began trembling and became tearful at such a statement from a man to whom all the people of the present generation are inferior in the matter of knowledge and piety. When he saw me in tears, he asked the reason for my tears. I said, “What wrong have I committed that you should say such a thing to me?”

Peter answered, “If it was wrong of me to speak of serving you, you were the first to do wrong, since you thought it proper to do this for me.”

I said, “It is not the same. It is entirely fitting for me to do this, but for you, the herald of God who saves our souls, it is a grievous thing to do this for me.”

Peter answered, “I would agree with you, except that our Lord, who came for the salvation of the whole world and who alone was noble above everyone, endured servitude so that he might persuade us not to be ashamed to perform servants’ services for our brothers, even if we happen to be exceedingly noble.”

I said, “If I think I can defeat you in argument, I am foolish. Nevertheless, I give thanks to God’s providence that I was deemed worthy to have you in the place of parents.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οἷον λόγον εἶπεν ἀνήρ, οὗ πάντες οἱ τῆς νῦν γενεᾶς ἄνθρωποι τῷ τῆς γνώσεως καὶ εὐσεβείας λόγῳ ἥττους τυγχάνουσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: at such a statement from a man to whom all the people of the present generation are inferior in the matter of knowledge and piety
lexical_decisions.rationale: οἷον gives the statement an emphatic quality. The second λόγῳ is taken as indicating the respect or matter in which the present generation is inferior rather than as naming a separate discourse.

lexical_decisions.chosen: serving you
lexical_decisions.rationale: The infinitive denotes performing a subordinate or servile role for Clement. “Serving” is natural here, while the stronger status nuance of the cognate δουλεία is represented by “servitude” later in the passage.

lexical_decisions.chosen: since you thought it proper to do this for me
lexical_decisions.rationale: The infinitive is understood with Clement as its subject: he had considered it fitting to perform such service for Peter. A more formal rendering would be “having deemed it worthy to do this for me.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Συνεθέμην ἂν σοι, ἐπεὶ ὁ κύριος ἡμῶν
lexical_decisions.chosen: I would agree with you, except that our Lord
lexical_decisions.rationale: The unreal “I would agree” is followed by the consideration that prevents agreement. Although ἐπεί commonly means “since,” its contextual force here can be expressed as “except that” or “were it not that.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: who alone was noble above everyone
lexical_decisions.rationale: εὐγενής can mean noble or well-born. The wording preserves the comparison with all others without specifying whether the author’s emphasis is social birth, inherent nobility, or both.

lexical_decisions.chosen: endured servitude
lexical_decisions.rationale: δουλεία denotes the condition or service of a servant or slave. “Servitude” preserves the stronger status nuance without specifying an episode not named by the source.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in the place of parents
lexical_decisions.rationale: The plural γονέων is retained: Clement regards Peter as occupying the place held collectively by his parents.

passages.text:
Peter asked, “Do you truly have no one related to you by birth?”

I answered, “There are indeed many prominent men of Caesar’s family. That is why Caesar himself, since my father had also been brought up with him, arranged for a female relative to be joined in marriage to my father. From her we were born, three sons: two before me, who were twins and were extremely like each other, as my father himself used to tell me. For I do not remember either them or the woman who bore me very well, but, as though through dreams, I call up a dim image of them.

“My mother, then, was called Mattidia, and my father Faustus. As for my brothers themselves, one was called Faustinus and the other Faustinianus. After I was born to them as their third child, my mother saw a dream—as my father used to recount—that unless she immediately took her twin sons and left the city of the Romans to live abroad for ten years, she was destined to die together with them by an utterly ruinous fate.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Οὐδεὶς δέ σου ἀληθῶς πρὸς γένος ὑπάρχει;
lexical_decisions.chosen: Do you truly have no one related to you by birth?
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρὸς γένος asks about kinship or family connection. “By birth” distinguishes this relationship from Peter’s preceding reference to brotherhood “according to God.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Εἰσὶν μὲν πολλοὶ καὶ μεγάλοι ἄνδρες, Καίσαρος πρὸς γένους ὄντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: There are indeed many prominent men of Caesar’s family
lexical_decisions.rationale: μεγάλοι describes the men as great or prominent, while Καίσαρος πρὸς γένους indicates family or kinship connection with Caesar.

lexical_decisions.chosen: since my father had also been brought up with him
lexical_decisions.rationale: σύντροφος can denote a childhood companion, foster-brother, or someone reared together with another. The rendering preserves shared upbringing without asserting formal fosterage.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐγὼ γὰρ οὔτε αὐτοὺς. οὔτε τὴν τεκοῦσαν πάνυ ἐπίσταμαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: For I do not remember either them or the woman who bore me very well
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπίσταμαι ordinarily means “know,” but the following reference to a dim mental image makes recollection the contextual sense. With the negation, πάνυ is represented as “very well.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὥσπερ δι᾿ ὀνείρων ἀμαυρὸν αὐτῶν τὸ εἶδος ἀναφέρω
lexical_decisions.chosen: as though through dreams, I call up a dim image of them
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀναφέρω here concerns bringing an image back to mind. The translation retains both the dreamlike comparison and the indistinctness of the remembered appearance.

lexical_decisions.chosen: unless she immediately took
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐξαυτῆς means “immediately” or “at once,” not “by herself.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πανολεθρίῳ μόρῳ ἅμα αὐτοῖς ἀποθανεῖν ἔχει
lexical_decisions.chosen: she was destined to die together with them by an utterly ruinous fate
lexical_decisions.rationale: πανολέθριος conveys complete ruin or destruction, μόρος can mean doom, fate, or death, and ἀποθανεῖν ἔχει expresses an impending or destined death. “By an utterly ruinous fate” preserves the source’s separate reference to doom without repeating “death” in English.

source_issues.source_quote: ἐγὼ γὰρ οὔτε αὐτοὺς. οὔτε τὴν τεκοῦσαν πάνυ ἐπίσταμαι
source_issues.issue: The printed period interrupts the correlative construction οὔτε … οὔτε. The translation treats the clauses as grammatically continuous while preserving all the printed words. This appears to be an editorial punctuation oddity rather than missing content.
source_issues.proposed_reading: ἐγὼ γὰρ οὔτε αὐτοὺς οὔτε τὴν τεκοῦσαν πάνυ ἐπίσταμαι

passages.text:
Our father, then, being devoted to his children, adequately supplied them for the journey with male and female servants, put them aboard a ship, and sent them away to Athens so that the boys would be educated together. But he kept only me, his son, with him as consolation. For this I give abundant thanks: that the dream had not commanded me too to leave the city of the Romans with my mother.

“When a year had passed, my father sent money to Athens for his own people and at the same time sent to learn how they were doing. But those who went did not return. In the third year my father, becoming despondent, likewise sent others with provisions. They came in the fourth year and reported that they had seen neither my mother nor my brothers, that the missing family had not even been in Athens itself, and that they had not found so much as a trace of anyone else who had gone away with them.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: being devoted to his children
lexical_decisions.rationale: φιλότεκνος describes strong affection for one’s children. “Devoted” suits both the father’s preparations and his subsequent search.

lexical_decisions.chosen: with male and female servants
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both the masculine and feminine forms are represented. In this household context they may denote enslaved attendants; “servants” follows the supplied wording policy while the possible bonded status remains disclosed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς τὰς Ἀθήνας ἅμα παιδευθησομένους ἐξέπεμψεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: sent them away to Athens so that the boys would be educated together
lexical_decisions.rationale: The masculine plural παιδευθησομένους most naturally refers to the twin sons rather than to their mother. ἅμα is taken as “together,” though “at the same time” is lexically possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐμὲ δὲ μόνον υἱὸν εἰς παραμυθίαν ἔσχεν μεθ᾿ ἑαυτοῦ
lexical_decisions.chosen: he kept only me, his son, with him as consolation
lexical_decisions.rationale: εἰς παραμυθίαν identifies Clement as a source of comfort or consolation after the others’ departure.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: χρήματα τοῖς αὐτοῦ ἅμα τε καὶ μαθεῖν τὸ πῶς διάγουσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: sent money to Athens for his own people and at the same time sent to learn how they were doing
lexical_decisions.rationale: τοῖς αὐτοῦ means “for his own people,” contextually the absent family. The agents sent to make inquiries are left implicit in this clause and become explicit in οἱ δὲ ἀπελθόντες, “those who went.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: that the missing family had not even been in Athens itself
lexical_decisions.rationale: Here the unexpressed subject is taken as Clement’s mother and brothers, because the searchers were sent to Athens and their report concerns the missing family. Alternatively, the continuing subject may be the searchers, reporting that they had not stayed or resided in Athens itself. The Greek does not explicitly mark a change of subject.

lexical_decisions.chosen: that they had not found so much as a trace
lexical_decisions.rationale: κἄν strengthens the negation: the searchers found not even a trace.

passages.text:
When my father heard these things, he became bewildered by his great grief. Not knowing where he should set out to search for them, he took me with him, went down to Portus, and repeatedly questioned many people about where each one had seen or heard of a shipwreck that had occurred four years earlier. One person named one place, another a different place. He in turn asked whether they had seen the body of a woman with young children washed ashore. . When those people said that they had seen many corpses in many places, my father groaned on hearing it. Yet, because his inward affections were in turmoil, he kept making irrational inquiries, since he was attempting to search so vast an expanse of sea. Still, he could be excused, because through his affection for those being sought he was being fed on empty hopes.

“And so, eventually, he placed me under guardians and left me in Rome when I was twelve years old. Then he himself went down to Portus in tears, boarded a ship, put out to sea, and departed on the search. From that time until this very day I have neither received any letters from him nor learned with certainty whether he is alive or dead. Rather, I suspect that he too has died somewhere, either overcome by grief or overtaken by shipwreck. The evidence for this is that it is now the twentieth year since then, and since that time I have heard no reliable news at all about him.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: to Portus
lexical_decisions.rationale: Πόρτος is treated as the proper name of Rome’s harbor rather than translated generically as “the port.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: a shipwreck that had occurred four years earlier
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase can designate a wreck from four years before the inquiry. A broader contextual alternative is “a shipwreck during the preceding four years.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: the body of a woman with young children washed ashore
lexical_decisions.rationale: βρέφη can denote infants or very young children. “Young children” avoids fixing their precise age, while ἐκβεβρασμένον depicts the woman’s body as cast or washed ashore.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν οὖν πολλὰ λεγόντων ἑωρακέναι πτώματα κατὰ πολλοὺς τόπους
lexical_decisions.chosen: When those people said that they had seen many corpses in many places
lexical_decisions.rationale: The neuter accusative plural πολλὰ is taken with the neuter accusative plural πτώματα, supported by their agreement and the parallel πολλοὺς τόπους. Alternatively, πολλὰ may attach adverbially to λεγόντων: “when those who spoke at length said that they had seen corpses in many places.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: because his inward affections were in turmoil
lexical_decisions.rationale: σπλάγχνα literally denotes inward organs and figuratively deep affections. “Inward affections” retains more of the source image than a purely abstract reference to emotion.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to search so vast an expanse of sea
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expression emphasizes the immense extent of sea that he was irrationally attempting to investigate.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῇ πρὸς τοὺς ζητουμένους στοργῇ ἐλπίσιν ἐβουκολεῖτο κεναῖς
lexical_decisions.chosen: through his affection for those being sought he was being fed on empty hopes
lexical_decisions.rationale: βουκολέω literally evokes feeding or tending a herd and can figuratively mean sustaining or beguiling someone with expectations. The main rendering preserves the feeding image; “he was beguiled by empty hopes” is a less image-retentive alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he placed me under guardians
lexical_decisions.rationale: φροντισταί are people charged with oversight or care. “Guardians” suits the care of a twelve-year-old, though “caretakers” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἤδη λοιπὸν ἔκτοτε εἰκοστὸν ἔτος ἐστίν
lexical_decisions.chosen: it is now the twentieth year since then
lexical_decisions.rationale: The ordinal expression is retained rather than converted into an exact modern elapsed-year count.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀφ’ ἧς οὐδεμίαν τινὰ περὶ αὐτοῦ ἀλήθειαν ἤκουσα
lexical_decisions.chosen: since that time I have heard no reliable news at all about him
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀφ’ ἧς is understood elliptically as “since that time” or “since that day,” extending the absence of information from the father’s departure to the present. ἀλήθεια here denotes true or dependable information rather than abstract truth.

source_issues.issue: The image-checked edition prints two dots separated by a space after ἐκβεβρασμένον. Their function remains uncertain: they may mark unavailable wording or may be an editorial punctuation oddity. The English retains exactly “. .” at this point and supplies no restoration. The edition prints the unassimilated spelling ἐνβάς. It is intelligible as the participle ordinarily normalized as ἐμβάς, “having boarded.” The printed form is verified and no missing wording is involved.

"translation_policy_text": "# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.
